title: Is This the First Corporate Psychopath? - Nautilus
gist: A new case study in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics argues that Jeronimus Cornelisz, who seized control of the shipwrecked Dutch East India Company vessel Batavia survivors in 1629, showed hallmarks of corporate psychopathy, possibly the first documented instance.

insights.claim: A power vacuum after the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia ran aground on the Abrolhos Islands in 1629 was filled by junior merchant Jeronimus Cornelisz, whose rule over roughly 200 survivors was barbarous.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates how leadership vacuums in resource-scarce organizations can be captured by predatory actors.
insights.locator: In 1629, the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia

insights.claim: A historical case study in the Asian Journal of Business Ethics concludes that Cornelisz's conduct bore all the hallmarks of corporate psychopathy, possibly the first such instance.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Frames corporate psychopathy as a long-standing governance risk, relevant to management-quality screening.
insights.locator: According to a new historical case study
